implementation_notes: ES2015 destructuring assignment is the exchange: the right-hand side is evaluated first, so [a, b] = [b, a] swaps two bindings without a temporary, and because JavaScript values are references this is all the classic C++ handle swap was for. There is no user-defined assignment, no copy constructor to allocate through and no noexcept to write, so what replaces the structure is simply "keep the mutable state behind one property (or one module-level binding) and rebind it"; rollback is the reverse assignment in a catch block, and the same expression works on array elements ([xs[i], xs[j]] = [xs[j], xs[i]]). Keep the exchange out of setters/getters, Proxies and frozen targets when it must not fail.
pitfalls: Destructuring allocates a temporary array on every exchange (GC pressure in hot loops); a plain `const t = a; a = b; b = t;` avoids that allocation when the swap is on the hot path.

Assigning through a setter, an accessor or a Proxy trap runs user code that can throw, and a two-property swap is not atomic: a failed second assignment leaves the object half exchanged, so only a single-property rebinding is a commit you can rely on.
Assignment to frozen objects, non-writable properties or const bindings throws in strict mode (and silently fails in sloppy mode), so a non-throwing helper must not assume writability.
There is no atomic exchange in the language: for state shared with workers or across realms, publish an immutable snapshot through a message or a single shared cell instead of swapping two fields.
